steps.prompt: Which version sounds smoother? What did the writer add?
steps.a: I wanted to go. It was raining. I stayed home. I read a book.
steps.b: I wanted to go, but it was raining, so I stayed home and read a book.
steps.reveal: “But”, “so” and “and” are coordinating conjunctions. They join ideas and show how they connect: a contrast (but), a result (so), an addition (and).

cards.title: Meet the FANBOYS
cards.body: The seven coordinating conjunctions spell FANBOYS: For (because), And (adds), Nor (adds a negative), But (contrast), Or (choice), Yet (surprising contrast), So (result). They join words, phrases or whole sentences of equal weight.

cards.title: The comma rule
cards.body: When FANBOYS joins two complete sentences (each with its own subject and verb), put a comma before it: “The hike was long, but the view was worth it.” When it joins two verbs that share one subject, no comma: “I ate breakfast and brushed my teeth.”

cards.title: Comma splice vs compound sentence
cards.telling: The bus was late, we missed the film.
cards.showing: The bus was late, so we missed the film.
cards.note: A comma alone can’t join two sentences. It needs a FANBOYS word to help.

cards.title: Don’t overdo “and”
cards.text:
We went to the beach and we swam and then we ate and then we went home. ✗
We went to the beach and swam. After lunch, we headed home. ✓
cards.note: A chain of “and then”s is tiring to read. Mix FANBOYS with full stops and other joining words.

prompts: Explain in your own words when you need a comma before “and” or “but”.
Which FANBOYS word do you use least? Write a sentence with it.
